entries.title: Judiciary Committee Delays Blanche Nomination Vote
entries.summary: Sen. John Cornyn said the acting attorney general and the Department of Justice have “stonewalled” his demands.
entries.content:
The Senate Judiciary Committee has officially delayed a vote on Todd Blanche’s nomination to become attorney general, as he struggles to secure the support of two key Senate Republicans.

Standing in the way of Blanche’s promotion from acting attorney general are Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina), with Cornyn saying that Blanche and the Justice Department haven’t done enough to ease his concerns over the proposed $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund and a deal shielding President Donald Trump from future tax audits.

“[Judiciary Chair Chuck Grassley] works to set President Trump’s nominees up for success in committee, not failure,” a spokesperson for the committee said. “Senators Cornyn and Tillis want written assurances from the Department of Justice regarding the Trump-IRS settlement. Tomorrow’s markup is postponed as work continues to secure sufficient support in committee to favorably report Attorney General-nominee Todd Blanche, who is highly qualified for the job.”

A “no” vote by either Cornyn or Tillis would likely doom Blanche’s nomination.

“They’ve stonewalled it,” Cornyn told reporters on Wednesday. “They’re making this a lot harder than it needs to be. … They claim to be negotiating in good faith, but something’s not working, and I don’t know where the problem is. We’re trying to make it easy on them. They simply refuse to take our help.”

The Texas Republican had hoped for a resolution Wednesday morning as he was scheduled to meet with Blanche, but instead he canceled that meeting, alleging that DOJ was not “responsive” to his asks — particularly on the scope of the tax audit proposal. He also said that he sent the Justice Department line-by-line edits to their proposal on the “anti-weaponization” fund and the audit immunity deal.

Later in the day, Cornyn huddled with Tillis and Grassley to brief them on the situation. Grassley delayed the vote hours later, with Cornyn continuing to wonder why Blanche’s team has not been sufficiently responsive.

“I would think [Blanche] wants to be confirmed,” Cornyn said. “I don’t think he’s going to be confirmed if he doesn’t at least try to be responsive.”

Cornyn has insisted Blanche put in writing that the anti-weaponization fund will not go forward, adding that Blanche’s word that it’s “dead” and “moot” is insufficient. Cornyn has noted repeatedly that the agreement between the IRS and the president could be revived later via a breach of contract lawsuit — meaning that a change must be made in writing.

Amid the tumult, Blanche held meetings elsewhere on Capitol Hill, including with Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah), another holdout if Blanche’s nomination were to make it out of the Judiciary committee, and Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyoming).

Cornyn, the former No. 2 Senate Republican, has long been an ally of leadership, but has been putting his new-found freedom to use after he lost his primary in May. He dispelled speculation on Wednesday that he will fall in line despite his ongoing skepticism of Blanche and the DOJ's deal with Trump. 

“Maybe they think they can roll me,” Cornyn told reporters, adding that’s not the case. 

Other Republicans on the committee think Cornyn will stick to his guns.

“If I were the Justice Department, I would believe him,” said Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana). “He’s as serious as four heart attacks and a stroke — and an aneurysm.”

The delay has major implications for Blanche, as it means his nomination process to become the full-time attorney general will spill beyond the August recess. Republican leaders had been hoping to get him over the finish line before they leave for the five-week break late next week.

entries.title: LCV Victory Fund Will Spend at Least $50 Million Backing Democrats
entries.summary: The climate group’s midterm push will focus on affordability and rising utility costs.
entries.content:
A leading progressive climate group is planning to spend at least $50 million on the 2026 midterms — a boost to Democrats looking to retake both chambers of Congress.

The LCV Victory Fund, the super PAC affiliated with the League of Conservation Voters, is targeting House Republican candidates in five battleground districts, with plans to expand that list heading into the fall, and will be boosting former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper of North Carolina and former Sen. Sherrod Brown of Ohio in their respective Senate bids. It will also spend on gubernatorial and state legislative races in Michigan, Nevada and Georgia — a trio of states with competitive down-ballot races.

The details of LCV Victory Fund were shared first with NOTUS.

The spending will go toward advertising, field programs and work with content creators. LCV Victory Fund is particularly targeting voters who feel the affordability pinch — voters who are more likely to be women, Black or Latino, noncollege educated and less politically engaged, said Sara Schreiber, LCV Victory Fund’s senior vice president of campaigns.

“A key part of the electorate is affected by this affordability crisis, and they are really looking for candidates who have plans and are creating solutions that will keep costs low,” Schreiber said in an interview with NOTUS. “These are the folks that you need to win in a midterm, and they're going to be critical in 2026.”

The eight-figure pledge is “on par” with previous midterm campaigns from the group, Schreiber said. During the 2022 cycle, LCV Victory Fund spent more than $40 million on independent expenditures and contributions to candidates.

LCV Victory Fund’s pledge comes as Democrats face a widening gap in fundraising between Democratic-aligned entities and Republican-backed groups. Some Democrats are concerned about the party’s ability to keep up with Republican spending in vital races. The Democratic National Committee, for example, remains in debt, while the Republican National Committee has built a $120 million war chest.

LCV Victory Fund’s ads — some of which started running earlier this month — drill Republicans on rising utility costs, complimenting House Democrats’ larger focus on affordability. In Michigan, LCV Victory Fund is out with a new ad attacking Republican Rep. Bill Huizenga for “votes to cut our clean energy supply” that “made our utility rates go up.”

Public polling suggests those attack lines could be effective, particularly around rising energy costs. Nearly two-thirds of voters said President Donald Trump’s policies have “worsened” economic conditions in the country in a CNN poll released this week. Nearly eight in 10 voters said the Trump administration is not focused enough on lowering prices in a recent CBS News poll.

LCV President Pete Maysmith called energy costs a “potent issue” for voters, one that already had success for Democrats in off-year victories in the New Jersey and Virginia gubernatorial elections.

“It’s the central message because Republicans have broken trust with voters,” Maysmith said. “They're causing real pain in people's pocketbooks, and that shows up both in their utility bills, which are up 18% since Trump took office, when he pledged to cut them in half.”

A handful of 2026 candidates are already leaning into utility cost messaging in their own ads.

Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford, who is running for governor, touted his record of suing “big utilities and drug companies to lower costs” in his first TV ad. In Pennsylvania, Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti, who is challenging Republican Rep. Rob Bresnahan, hit data centers for “raising our electric bills” in her ad.

entries.title: Want to Play Doubles With Venus Williams? The Correct Answer Is Yes.
entries.summary: In a last-minute pairing, the 46-year-old tennis legend played alongside 22-year-old Diana Shnaider at this week’s D.C. Open.
entries.content:
The most impressive athletic feat anyone has pulled off so far at the Mubadala D.C. Open didn’t occur on a tennis court, but on the leafy walkways and concourses connecting the tournament’s corporate offices to the players’ area. It was performed not by a tennis player but by the tournament’s longtime chair, Mark Ein, who covered those several hundred yards — in dress shoes and sport coat, his cell phone pressed to his ear — well, faster than anyone could have reasonably expected from a 61-year-old.

Ein, at that instant, was on a desperate mission to salvage a sizable chunk of the tournament’s star factor.

It was 1:10 p.m. Saturday and Ein had just gotten a call from Andrea Preti, the husband of tennis legend Venus Williams, informing him that Williams’ intended doubles partner, Alexandra Eala, had scratched at the eleventh hour. With the 2 p.m. deadline for doubles entries looming, they had 50 minutes and ticking to find Williams a replacement. Ein didn’t wait to finish the call before rushing out his office door and down the walkways.

Upon bursting into the players’ dining area, the first person he saw was Diana Shnaider, a 22-year-old Russian and the 18th-ranked women’s tennis player in the world, having lunch with her support team.

“Diana,” Ein said, catching his breath, “how would you like to play doubles this week with Venus Williams?”

For the roughly 3,000 fans who crammed into the outlying John Harris Court at the Rock Creek Park Tennis Center on Monday for an up-close glimpse of tennis royalty — the 46-year-old Williams owns seven Grand Slam singles titles and another 14 in doubles — then crammed in again Wednesday evening for their quarterfinal match, they have Ein’s resourcefulness and Shnaider’s intrepidness to thank for the experience.

And Williams, on a miserable run of bad luck with her choice of doubles partners of late, may have just accidentally hit upon a solution to her problem.

Despite having never played together before, Williams and Shnaider demonstrated an uncanny degree of chemistry in winning Monday’s first-round match, 6-3, 6-4, over American Quinn Gleason and Norway’s Ulrikke Eikeri, before falling in Wednesday night’s quarterfinals to Chinese duo Qianhui Tang and Yifan Xu, 6-4, 6-2.

Venus Williams AP - 26211029058450 (4943x3293, AR: 1.50)
If one thing has defined the first half of this year’s D.C. Open, it is the slow bleed-off of A-list American stars, both male and female, from the tournament draw. Among those joining Williams in departing well short of the weekend are hometown legend and sixth seed Frances Tiafoe; fifth-seeded Learner Tien, the 16th-ranked men’s player in the world; and Madison Keys, the 2025 Australian Open champ and sixth seed in the women’s draw. All lost their first-round matches.

For Williams, as with many American players, the D.C. stop on the North American hard-court circuit holds a special place in her heart. It’s no coincidence she chose this tournament as the site of her own return to the game last summer following a 16-month absence. (Her singles victory here a year ago over Peyton Stearns at age 45 made her the second-oldest player in history to win a singles match, but she is 0-12 since in singles, including a loss Tuesday night to Austria’s Anastasia Potapova. Williams entered Wednesday ranked 664th in the world in singles, 124th in doubles.)

“You can just feel it from the fans,” Williams said. “They’re ride or die.”

To the extent that Williams’ radiance permitted anyone to pay attention to Shnaider, they would have noticed, above all else, the incredulous smile that seemed to be plastered across the young Russian’s face between points and during changeovers. It was the same smile that Ein encountered on Saturday — “Absolutely giddy,” he described her — when he presented the offer of being Williams’ partner.

“It was definitely the right choice,” Shnaider said of her decision to accept. “I feel like it was definitely a great partnership.”

Paradoxically, playing doubles these days with Williams — among the most decorated players of her generation and, along with sister Serena, half of the second-most-prolific doubles team in history — is both an intimidating notion for a young player and an egalitarian rite of passage, open to just about any current WTA player with a racket and a halfway decent world ranking.

In the four-plus years since Serena famously stepped away from the sport — a decision she would eventually reverse, also famously, this summer — Venus has found it almost impossible to find a full-time doubles partner. Her last seven tournaments have seen her paired with seven different partners, and she only found herself scrambling at the last minute to find a new partner this week because Eala, with whom Williams partnered last month at a tournament in Germany, pulled out in order to focus on her singles matches.

(Williams’s eleventh-hour switch from Eala to Shnaider was described by tournament officials as a “repairing,” which is the sort of beautiful euphemism that would seem to have enormous potential for divorce lawyers.)

Diana Shnaider AP - 26211029468275 (5392x3592, AR: 1.50)
Eala’s late scratch extended a brutal streak of rotten luck for Williams in recent doubles competition. In May, American up-and-comer Hailey Baptiste scratched out of their planned French Open pairing with a knee injury. Then, at last month’s Wimbledon, where Serena launched her comeback and where the Williams sisters secured a wild-card entry in doubles, Serena injured her knee during her first-round singles loss to Maya Joint and was forced to withdraw from doubles. Then came Eala’s last-minute decision to withdraw in D.C.

“It’s just unlucky. Time and unforeseen circumstances befall us all,” Williams said. “I would like to hopefully get lucky.”

It’s not as if Williams is an undesirable or unsavory doubles partner. Shnaider’s eagerness to pair with her this week speaks to Williams’ magnetic pull on younger players. So do the words offered this week by Leylah Fernandez, who has played doubles with Williams twice, including at the 2025 U.S. Open.

“It's tough [playing with Williams], because I knew how competitive she was and how much she loves winning and hates losing. I was stressed, I was nervous,” Fernandez said. “What I didn't know was [her ability] to calm me down. … Venus definitely has a welcoming aura where she always wants to support and help as much as possible. It motivates me. It encourages me, and it brings me back to why I play tennis.”

On Wednesday evening, at the instant their loss was sealed, Williams and Shnaider met on their side of the net and shared a good, long hug. The adoring crowd, by this point well thinned out, stood and cheered and snapped photos, just in case it might be the last time they see Williams in these parts.

But she doesn’t sound like someone who is ready to bow out. She spoke of her hopes for a delayed reunion with Serena in U.S. Open doubles later this summer, provided Serena is healthy. And despite the chaos of this week — a “repairing,” an unfamiliar partner, a riveting win, a gutting loss — she sounded like someone who wouldn’t want it any other way.

“In tennis, you're learning something about yourself every day. It just doesn't end,” Williams said. “It's such a beautiful and sometimes painful discovery, and I look forward to every day of it.”

entries.title: Janeese Lewis George Has Been Meeting With Her Critics
entries.summary: In recent days, the Democratic nominee for D.C. mayor met with a business organization and the D.C. Police Union.
entries.content:
You could call it fence-mending, extending an olive branch, opening lines of communication, or simply municipal diplomacy. Whatever it is, it’s happening.

Over the last week, Democratic D.C. mayoral nominee Janeese Lewis George has met with a prominent business organization as well as the leadership of the D.C. Police Union, engaging in conversations with two groups that have expressed unease with — if not outright hostility toward — her progressive proposals.

The outreach marks the very early days of what campaign aides don’t yet want to call a mayoral transition; Lewis George still has the November general election ahead of her, after all.

But after her decisive victory in the District’s June 16 primary, in which she won with 54% of the vote and all but ensured she’ll be the next mayor of the overwhelmingly Democratic city, there is consensus that Lewis George has to start laying the groundwork now for what will be a significant shift in priorities and policies if and when she takes office in January.

“There is a sense of urgency here,” says Ward 6 Council member Charles Allen, who has been advising Lewis George’s post-primary efforts. “We have a lot of work ahead of us, and any candidate who won with a massive mandate would be champing at the bit to be engaged. She has been incredibly busy since the election.”

Campaign aides say Lewis George has been “meeting with tons of groups,” including those that were part of her winning coalition: teachers, environmentalists, tenants and immigrant rights organizations. But the aides — who spoke on the condition of anonymity so they could comment on internal campaign matters — say say she also has spoken with housing providers, developers and CEOs.

“It was a tough primary, and she’s reaching out to people on all sides, including people not in her camp,” one aide said.

One of those meetings happened this week with a small group of executives who are part of the Greater Washington Partnership, which represents large employers from Baltimore down to Richmond.

The meeting is notable because the business community more broadly backed Kenyan McDuffie in the primary, seeing him as a more reliable quantity — a continuation of Bowser, to a certain degree.

Some business leaders are concerned that Lewis George’s policies won’t help revive and diversify D.C.’s economy, and that proposals for possible tax increases could instead drive employers to Maryland and Virginia. There is particular worry around a Business Activity Tax, which would target law firms, lobbyists and consulting firms whose owners live outside the city.

Some have said they need to impress upon Lewis George how challenging D.C.’s business climate has gotten. “I couldn’t raise a dime now if I tried,” said one real estate developer, who, like others, spoke on the condition of anonymity.

Others, though, are more encouraged by Lewis George’s promise to work with universities and other institutions to help revitalize downtown D.C., as well as her pledge to cut red tape and bureaucracy that can complicate housing construction and running a business in the city. One person in the world of finance and investment said approaching Lewis George openly is better than simply assuming the worst of her.

“We can’t walk in saying, ‘We don’t like this,’ without saying, ‘This is what success looks like,’” the person said.

Kathy Hollinger, the CEO of the partnership, tells NOTUS that the meeting with Lewis George was intended to open lines of communication and press the argument that D.C. is a vital component of the region’s economy — but that companies, like residents, have choices in where they locate.

“The conversation was an encouraging first step in establishing what we expect will be a needed relationship,” Hollinger said. “These were CEOs from the region’s most significant private sector industries together with leading universities, health systems and nonprofit institutions. We shared with her very directly that just those who were around the table employ more than 70,000 people in the District. Many of the priorities discussed included housing, affordability, permitting and downtown revitalization.”

At-Large Council member Elissa Silverman, a fellow progressive who during her career has clashed and worked with the business community, said the outreach is necessary — and can be mutually beneficial.

“I think there’s a lot of room to make the rules less bureaucratic, more understandable, better both for business and the economy,” she said. “The change in administration is an opportunity to reimagine programs that haven’t had scrutiny or a good look taken in a while.”

Lewis George also met last week with the leadership of the D.C. Police Union, which represents more than 3,000 police officers.

The union has been highly critical of Lewis George and the D.C. Council in the past; union leaders have aggressively pushed Republicans in Congress to intervene in the city’s local affairs and broadly supported President Donald Trump’s move last year to deploy the National Guard in the city. Lewis George and other lawmakers have been critical of both stances.

Lewis George has promised to end any cooperation between MPD and ICE on her first day in office. She has also endorsed non-police approaches to fighting crime, but has generally backed away from her support in 2019 and 2020 for defunding the police.

The tension between the two camps was evident in how the meeting was set up: Lewis George asked that the D.C. firefighters union, which endorsed her during the primary, make the initial outreach on her behalf. (Dozens of unions backed Lewis George; the police union did not make an endorsement.)

Police union President Gregg Pemberton did not respond to requests for comment on the meeting with Lewis George, and her campaign aides said little about what was discussed. “It was a positive meeting,” one offered. “It was introductory. There will be more to come.”

The next D.C. mayor will immediately be faced with a big decision for MPD: who to appoint as chief. Current Police Chief Jeffery Carroll remains in an interim capacity, and Bowser is unlikely to nominate him for the permanent post considering the upcoming change in administrations.

The next mayor will also have to handle what has been a persistent issue with the department: staffing. As of this month, there are some 3,157 sworn officers in MPD, down from roughly 3,800 a decade ago. The lower number of officers and increased demands on their time has led to record overtime budgets. In the 2025 fiscal year, for example, the department spent $134 million on overtime pay.

Ultimately, though, Lewis George’s campaign aides say they’re entering the meetings they have with the election’s results in mind — and trying to find ways to bring critics on board.

“There are mandates for universal access to affordable child care, to build tens of thousands of homes, to lower utility prices, and to end cooperation with ICE,” said one aide who spoke to NOTUS. “How do we deliver on them on day 1 or year 1? That starts by bringing in as many players while also continuing the conversations and relationships with our base.”

entries.title: Talk to Tom: What Is the Best Tasting Menu in D.C.?
entries.summary: Tom Sietsema answers reader questions on restaurant bread baskets, tipping etiquette and a go-to Baltimore steakhouse.
entries.content:
Welcome to Talk to Tom, the dining advice column that aims to point you toward good meals, steer you from the dross and solve your pressing restaurant queries. Look for a fresh Q&A every Thursday in this space. 

Questions and comments can be submitted to TalkToTom@notus.com. Submissions may be edited for length and clarity.

If I get comped for something, like a drink or appetizer, and it wasn’t because something was wrong, how should that be reflected in my tip? 

There are a couple of schools of thought on the matter, and my answer depends in part on a diner’s relationship with a restaurant. One response is to tip as if you ordered the item. What server won’t appreciate that?

More often than not, however, something gratis is going out to a guest who is celebrating a special occasion or who makes regular appearances. In those situations, industry pros tell me, the gift should be considered what it is: a gesture of hospitality that requires no more reciprocation than a “thank you very much.”

Restaurants deal with leftovers differently. Do you prefer to box unfinished food yourself or have staff take care of the task?

Some places want diners to do the job, because diners know exactly what leftovers they want. (I’ve heard stories about customers getting upset because, for instance, cleaned steak bones and tiny garnishes weren’t included in their bags of leftovers.)

Personally, I appreciate places that handle the matter behind the scenes; that’s part of hospitality. Have you ever tried to transfer a big piece of unfinished meat or slippery noodles from plate or bowl to take-out container, sometimes without proper serving utensils? Not so easy, or neat.

I also like it when a server instructs you to retrieve your leftovers at the host stand, on the way out, versus plopping a bag on your table or the floor while you’re still there. At the fun new steakhouse Ox & Olive in Georgetown, servers give you a playing card to remember food to go. Guests pick up the bags that match their cards from a cute wooden “tree” at the entrance.

It feels like tasting menus are getting long again. 

Ah, you must have heard me grouse about the time I sat for over three hours at a D.C. hotspot and ended up taking home 99 percent of the pastry chef’s multiple desserts because I simply couldn’t eat ONE. MORE. THING. While much of the food was very good, the flurry of dishes felt like a forced march, as though the chef wanted to pack all his ideas into one epic seating. By the end of the night, I felt as if I had dispatched a Thanksgiving’s worth of food and drink (and wished I had stretch pants on). My one-word review would have read, “Uncomfortable.”

But I digress. The opposite of that night occurred just last week, at Rooster & Owl on 14th Street Northwest, where chef Yuan Tang offers what might be my favorite tasting menu in D.C. One, it’s four courses, with multiple choices. Two, the cost is $125, a value given the quality, creativity and competition around town. Three, the meal is paced perfectly, so there never seems to be a rush or a lag. Two of us were in and out in about 90 minutes. We left sated but not stuffed, and eager to return.
DC0A6147 copy 2.jpg (7000x5215, AR: 1.34)Tang’s new menu speaks to the season and makes me wonder how, for instance, cantaloupe might be rethought as dan dan noodles, crab fritters would taste with spiced honey, pork skewers could be embellished with fish sauce gastrique, and mango sticky rice gets fused with a pavlova. My long history with the upscale mom-and-pop forecasts that everything will be on point — and my recent reunion proved as much.

My pet peeve continues to be loud restaurants. Why do so many of them sound like boom boxes?

In many restaurants, the culprit is in the design: lots of glass, metal and exposed brick, sometimes in combination with bare concrete floors and high ceilings. Hard surfaces reflect sound, rather than absorb it.

A packed dining room increases the noise, too, as customers raise their voices to be heard, a phenomenon known as the Lombard effect. The problem is exacerbated when restaurants crank up their playlists, thinking loud music creates a sought-after buzz. Open bars and kitchens, with their distinct sound effects — espresso machines, clanging pots, ice bins — also contribute to the noise pollution.

Restaurants can lower the volume by installing acoustic panels, curtains, rugs or even artwork designed to sponge noise; adding more space between tables; selecting softer finishes; and measuring sound levels rather than relying on instinct. (There are apps for that, don’t you know.) An average of between 65 to 70 decibels should be the aim.

For their part, diners ISO peace with their meals should consider eating on the early side, asking for tables on the perimeter of dining rooms — and letting their voices be heard by management. Wouldn’t it be great if more restaurants offered something along the lines of a designated music- and phone-free time period for people who don’t want to read lips or shout throughout dinner?

Research has shown that excessive noise can shorten restaurant visits and increase stress — not exactly agreeable outcomes for anyone.

My grandson is about to turn 18. We’re in Baltimore and steak is on his wish list. 

A big birthday (your progeny can vote now!) calls for something special. The place that leaps to mind is the family-owned Prime Rib, launched in 1965 and as popular for its ambience — tuxedoed servers, live piano, retro supper club look — as for its succulent, signature cut, which diners should order cooked medium-rare and eat with grated horseradish.

It seems service is inevitably worse in a restaurant that’s slow. Your take? 

You’d think a slow dining room would translate to more customer attention, but that’s not necessarily the case. A busy restaurant creates momentum and buzz; in a nearly empty one, staff can become less focused because there’s no rhythm to the service.

To control labor costs, during slow periods restaurants might schedule fewer workers — servers who might then take on multiple tasks, including answering the phone, greeting and seating guests, busing tables and maybe bar tending. Management might also ask them to help with duties like stocking, napkin-folding or food preparation, which can distract them from their primary job of looking after customers. Morale also takes a hit in a slow restaurant, with servers worried about tips and schedules. Places that struggle to attract business might have a hard time hiring and keeping good workers.

To be clear, good restaurants can be slow for reasons unrelated to quality. Bad weather and traffic jams, for instance, can wreak havoc on reservations and walk-in customers.

Given high prices, my rant is restaurants that charge for bread service. It immediately turns me off. I long for the bread baskets at Le Diplomate or Obelisk.  

The reality is, the complimentary gestures at those establishments cost a lot, in terms of labor and/or money, and this in an industry with particularly thin margins. At Le Diplomate, the beloved French brasserie on 14th Street Northwest, chef Greg Lloyd tells me the amenity — a basket brimming with slices of baguette, rye wheat boule and cranberry-walnut loaf, served with lightly salted whipped butter — costs the restaurant $250,000 a year. As for the fixed-price Obelisk, Esther Lee, the chef-owner of the intimate Italian townhouse in Dupont Circle, says her grissini and other breads aren’t so much about the expense of ingredients, but the time it takes the small business to produce them in-house.

A bread basket is more than a way to stave off hunger before the first course. It’s a way to signal care and craftsmanship — a welcome handshake, if you will. Gratis bread baskets haven’t exactly gone the way of pay phones. I’ve been offered them at restaurants as diverse as Ristorante i Ricchi and Joe’s Seafood, Prime Steak & Stone Crab downtown, Filomena Ristorante in Georgetown and Et Voila! in the Palisades. (Readers, help me grow this list, which I can share in a future column.)

To cut waste, the owner of I Ricchi, Chris Ricchi, says her gratis schiacciata, baked in the restaurant and adding to the Tuscan experience, is preceded by a question: Would you like bread? At Et Voila!, the Belgian restaurant offers the first basket free and charges $3.50 for a second.

entries.title: Paige Cognetti Refuses Corporate PAC Money. But Some Is Arriving Indirectly.
entries.summary: The Democratic candidate in a hot Pennsylvania congressional race has accepted money from political groups that are themselves funded by corporate PACs.
entries.content:
Paige Cognetti, the mayor of Scranton, Pennsylvania, who Democrats hope will unseat Republican Rep. Rob Bresnahan this November, has repeatedly pledged not to take money from corporate political action committees as a candidate or lawmaker.

“No Corporate PAC Money. As a candidate and member of Congress I will reject the influence of special interests,” Cognetti wrote on her campaign website.

But federal campaign finance filings show Cognetti has accepted donations from numerous political committees that themselves are awash in cash from corporate PACs, including money from defense contractor Boeing, banking giant JPMorgan Chase and insurance company UnitedHealthcare.

Many of the non-corporate political committees supporting Cognetti are leadership PACs operated by Democratic federal lawmakers to boost their party’s congressional candidates.

During her 2026 campaign to represent Pennsylvania’s 8th Congressional District, Cognetti has, for example, taken $5,000 from Blue Hen Federal PAC, a committee sponsored by Sen. Chris Coons (D-Delaware).

Coons’ committee has received hundreds of thousands of dollars this election cycle from a who’s who of corporate and trade association PACs tied to companies such as Visa, FedEx, Pfizer, Northrop Grumman, Eli Lilly,Google, McKinsey and Fox News parent Fox Corp., among several dozen others.

Cognetti’s campaign has also received $4,000 from the campaign committee of House Democratic Whip Katherine Clark, which itself is partly bankrolled by numerous corporate PACs, including those sponsored by Delta Air Lines, Verizon, Allstate Insurance and law and lobbying firm Alston & Bird.

Cognetti took money from dozens of these leadership PACs that report significant corporate contributions — including the PACs of Rep. Ted Lieu, the House Democratic Caucus vice chair, and Rep. Nancy Pelosi, the former speaker.

“Paige is the only candidate in this race who does not accept donations from corporate PACs, supports a federal ban on corporate PAC donations, and will never be handed a corporate check in exchange for special access or political favors,” Emma Mustion, the campaign’s communications director, said. “The reason for her pledge is simple: Paige is independent and doesn’t work for anybody but the people of Northeastern Pennsylvania.”

Cognetti’s pledge to reject corporate PAC money has become a key feature of her campaign, and is cited in endorsements from advocacy groups such as End Citizens United and lawmakers including Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Arizona).

Campaign finance and other money matters are key issues in the race between Cognetti and Bresnahan. Cognetti has repeatedly hit Bresnahan, who accepts direct corporate PAC money, for his once-prolific stock trading — the multimillionaire with his own helicopter made more than 650 individual stock trades during 2025, according to federal records.

Among them, he traded stock in companies that manage Medicaid just before the House took its first vote on Republicans’ sweeping tax cut bill that slashed the program. He has also personally invested in artificial intelligence companies before advocating for data centers.

NOTUS previously reported that Bresnahan abruptly stopped trading stocks earlier this year. At the time, a spokesperson said a financial institution managed Bresnahan’s stock trades.

“Only a slick politician like Paige Cognetti would make a promise to reject corporate PAC money a centerpiece of her campaign only to find a loophole to accept it,” Samantha Bullock, a spokesperson for Bresnahan’s campaign, said in a statement to NOTUS.
RobBresnahan1 (4667x3116, AR: 1.50)Federal records show Cognetti had $3.4 million cash on hand, besting Bresnahan’s $2.6 million war chest, as of June 30. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates the race between Bresnahan and Cognetti as a toss-up. National Republicans and Democrats alike consider the race critical to winning a House majority in 2027.

Cognetti, for her part, continues to run on an anti-corruption platform that includes banning members of Congress from trading individual stocks, instituting term limits for federal lawmakers, withholding lawmakers’ pay throughout government shutdowns and prohibiting members of Congress from making bets in prediction markets.

Other candidates have been criticized in the past for accepting similar contributions. Democrat Abigail Spanberger, now the governor of Virginia, campaigned on rejecting corporate PAC money while running for Congress in 2022 — and was slammed at the time for taking money from leadership PACs.

entries.title: Democrats Want to Avoid an Election Season Shutdown
entries.summary: “No one wants a shutdown in October,” said Sen. Patty Murray, Democrats’ top appropriator.
entries.content:
Democrats only have one major leverage point left against the Trump administration — and they're not about to use it.

With Congress approaching a government funding cliff at the end of September, key Senate Democrats signaled they want to take the threat of a government shutdown off the table. Several told NOTUS this week that they are open to a short-term stopgap spending measure to get through the election.

“If we can come up with a good bipartisan [continuing resolution], that would be great,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer told NOTUS.

Last year, Democrats forced a record-breaking 43-day government shutdown over expiring Obamacare tax credits, and earlier this year, the Department of Homeland Security was shut down for months due to a fight over immigration enforcement and Immigration and Customs Enforcement funding.

But on the verge of an election in which Democrats hope to retake power in the Capitol, they seem ready to punt the issue.

“We certainly want to avoid a government shutdown, and Democrats have been very clear about that,” Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland), a member of the Senate Appropriations Committee, told NOTUS on Wednesday. Van Hollen was one of the Democrats last year who blocked GOP attempts to reopen the government during the record-breaking shutdown. “We hope that Republicans will negotiate in good faith.”

Democrats in both chambers bristled at the opening salvo in funding negotiations from the GOP last week. House Republicans passed a short-term funding package that would kick the shutdown deadline to December. Democrats have panned the bill, arguing it doesn’t include adequate restrictions on how Trump administration officials could move funding around. Democrats have also laid out a red line that they will not approve additional funding for ICE without concessions on reforms from the White House.

Sen. Patty Murray (D-Washington), the top Democrat on the Appropriations panel, said Wednesday that she is working with Senate Republicans to draft a short-term funding measure into December that would “fix the problems with the bill that the House Republicans drafted.” Republicans need the support of at least seven Senate Democrats to pass any government funding package to avoid a filibuster.

“No one wants a shutdown in October,” Murray said.

Sen. Katie Britt (R-Alabama), another member of the Appropriations Committee, told NOTUS this week that she is “cautiously optimistic” about the status of government funding talks.

“I appreciate at this point people engaging in a meaningful way, which truly seems to be what's occurring,” Britt said.

Murray said Wednesday that a short-term deal would give lawmakers time to negotiate full spending bills for 2027. The government will shut down at the end of September without the passage of spending bills or a stopgap measure.

Progressive grassroots groups have heavily criticized congressional Democrats for failing to stand up to the Trump administration, urging them to get more aggressive in opposing the president’s budget.

"Democrats should use every ounce of leverage they have to protect their constituents and lower costs for working families — including continuing to hold the line against any additional funding for ICE or Border Patrol without ironclad guardrails,” Andrew O’Neill, director of advocacy at the progressive group Indivisible, said in a statement.

Pushing some Democrats toward a bipartisan compromise is the threat from Republican leaders to use the budget reconciliation process to fund the government. Reconciliation requires just a majority vote for passage and skips a potential filibuster in the Senate. Republicans earlier this year used that process to fund ICE and Border Protection, despite Democratic objections. That move would cut Democrats out of the funding talks altogether.

“It’s a bit of a pick-your-poison moment,” said Minnesota Sen. Tina Smith, acknowledging concerns about another Republican reconciliation package.

But other Democrats are still grappling with how to proceed on government funding given the Trump administration’s recent admission in court that it canceled grants for clean energy programs that Congress approved solely based on whether states voted for Trump in the 2024 election.

“We now know this unequivocally, that the president of the United States is withholding money from states for purely political reasons, not any other reason, and New Jersey is being shortchanged significantly,” said New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker. “This is unconscionable what’s happening right now.”

entries.title: JLG Holds Court
entries.content:
Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: Janeese Lewis George meets with campaign foes, a veteran sues the National Guard and Dulles Airport gets a makeover. 

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.




THE LATEST

Oh, to be a fly on the wall in that meeting.

Janeese Lewis George, winner of last month’s Democratic mayoral primary, recently met with the leadership of the D.C. Police Union, which was highly critical of her during the hotly contested campaign.

The meeting — brokered by the firefighters union, which endorsed her — was part of what Lewis George’s aides do not yet want to call a mayoral transition, but is an effort to lay the groundwork for the significant shift in priorities and policies that will take place if and when she takes office in January.

“There is a sense of urgency here,” said Ward 6 council member Charles Allen, who has been advising Lewis George’s post-primary efforts. “We have a lot of work ahead of us, and any candidate who won with a massive mandate would be champing at the bit to be engaged.”

That includes meetings with friends and foes alike to try to find common ground — or at least open channels of communication, NOTUS’ Martin Austermuhle reports. Other than the D.C. Police Union, Lewis George recently sat down with a small group from the Greater Washington Partnership, which represents large employers in the region.

The business community has been especially concerned about what Lewis George will do in office, though some leaders think it’s best to keep an open mind. “We can’t walk in saying, ‘We don’t like this,’ without saying, ‘This is what success looks like,’” said one local business leader.

Lewis George’s aides say they believe winning the primary with 54% of the vote gave her a broad mandate, and they are still focusing on her plans to try to bring down prices of child care and utilities, build more housing and end police cooperation with ICE.





DEEP DIVE

A veteran alleges that National Guard troops assaulted her outside her D.C. home, and she’s asking for $3 million in damages. Anna King said she was sitting on her front patio, scrolling on her phone, when National Guard troops walked onto the property and violently detained her, restraining her with handcuffs so tight that she tore at least one ligament in her wrist and required surgery. The ACLU of D.C. posted a video of the interaction, which happened in May.

King filed a tort claim with the Idaho National Guard and the Defense Department on Wednesday. She has been a vocal critic of the Guard’s presence in the District, and was detained in May over an accusation of assaulting Guard members two days earlier. She was never charged in that case, but has been charged with assault over the incident on her patio.

A spokesperson for the Idaho National Guard declined to comment on the specific allegations in King’s tort claim, citing the pending litigation, but said the Guard takes “all allegations of misconduct seriously.” The Defense Department did not provide comment.

Michael Perloff, a senior staff attorney at the ACLU of D.C., which is helping to represent King, told NOTUS the incident shows that National Guard troops have been acting like police. “Military members are trained for war,” he said. “There shouldn't be people who are trained for war policing the streets in American cities.”





FROM THE DISTRICT

Revving up: Mayor Muriel Bowser hopes next month’s Freedom 250 Grand Prix will be the first in a series of IndyCar races in D.C., she said at a press conference Wednesday.

“Let’s see how it goes this year,” responded Penske president Bud Denker, who is chairing the race. Denker estimated the event, scheduled for Aug. 22 and 23, will see “about 140,000 people a day come through the gates.”





FROM VIRGINIA

President Donald Trump announced a $22 billion renovation of the “really horribly thought of” Dulles International Airport in a Wednesday press conference, promising to add more than 5 million square feet of new or renovated space, NOTUS’ Jenna Monnin reports. The airport will also get a new 32,000-space parking garage and do away with its famous “people movers.” United Airlines will help fund the project.





FROM MARYLAND

The Education Department threatened this week to yank federal funds from Anne Arundel County Public Schools after parents complained a high school helped “their daughter pretend to be male,” The Washington Post reports.





TALK TO TOM

Rooster and Owl (8192x5462, AR: 1.50)
Tom Sietsema is back answering your questions about the D.C. dining scene. Submit your questions here.

Question: Is it just me, or are tasting menus getting longer? 

Ah, you must have heard me grouse about the time I sat for over three hours at a D.C. hotspot and ended up taking home 99% of the pastry chef’s multiple desserts because I simply couldn’t eat ONE. MORE. THING. While much of the food was very good, the flurry of dishes felt like a forced march, as though the chef wanted to pack all his ideas into one epic seating. By the end of the night, I felt as if I had dispatched a Thanksgiving’s worth of food and drink (and wished I had stretch pants on). My one-word review would have read, “Uncomfortable.”

But I digress. The opposite of that night occurred just last week, at Rooster & Owl on 14th Street Northwest, where chef Yuan Tang offers what might be my favorite tasting menu in D.C. One, it’s four courses, with multiple choices. Two, the cost is $125, a value given the quality, creativity and competition around town. Three, the meal is paced perfectly, so there never seems to be a rush or a lag. Two of us were in and out in about 90 minutes. We left sated but not stuffed, and eager to return.

In the full Q&A: Why slow restaurants sometimes provide worse service, how to tip on a comped item and the gradual disappearance of free bread. 





SPORTS

Training camp update: NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson was out at Day 1 of Commanders training camp Wednesday, and he reports it was a great opening session for the defense. Linebacker Odafe Oweh, the team’s biggest offseason addition, was disruptive whenever he was on the field, and there were near interceptions by Mike Sainristil and Jordan Magee.

Daronte Jones, the team’s new defensive coordinator, is a football nomad with roots in rural Maryland. The Athletic’s Barry Svrluga profiles the 47-year-old tasked with getting Washington’s defense back into shape.

entries.content:
Today’s notice: The stuff redacted from Fauci’s journal in the last few days will surprise you. Todd Blanche’s confirmation vote delayed. Centrist Democrat vs. Centrist Democrat in Michigan. More green spending. And: Chris Murphy wants answers on the civics contest controversy.





THE LATEST

Anthony Fauci and the Millers: Former Trump administration official Katie Miller, wife of top White House adviser Stephen Miller, is publicly one of Fauci’s harshest critics, joining in conservative calls for him to be imprisoned for his work during the COVID-19 pandemic. But NOTUS’ Margaret Manto reports that Fauci’s journal, released by Sen. Rand Paul (R-Kentucky) ahead of yesterday’s blockbuster Senate hearing, reveals a different side to their relationship in the scary, early days of COVID.

“Tonight she had an anxiety reaction. I calmed her over the phone,” Fauci wrote of Katie Miller in an entry dated May 9, 2020. The journal entry said, “I am calling katie frequently to check on her couple time per day. She is very anxious about getting very ill since she is 10 weeks pregnant.”

In the entries, Fauci writes about providing medical advice to the family on several occasions, including when both Katie and Stephen contracted the virus.

These entries were public, but now they’re not. They were in Paul’s original document dump, but some entries were heavily redacted at some point between their release Saturday and yesterday. The original documents mentioned Katie Miller 56 times, while the redacted documents mentioned her 37 times. Paul’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

Katie’s explanation: She told Margaret yesterday that she purposely gave Fauci the impression that she was friendly with him so that he “did not leak against me or my husband.”

“He was not my doctor. He was not my friend,” Katie told NOTUS. “He was a work colleague who called me for work purposes, and in the course of a phone call, you would discuss other things.”

From the Hill


Todd Blanche’s confirmation grinds to a halt. For now, at least. The Senate Judiciary Committee has delayed a vote on the acting attorney general’s nomination to drop the acting from the title. Republican Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Cornyn of Texas still haven’t agreed to vote for Blanche. An actual “no” vote from either of them would probably tank the nomination, NOTUS’ Al Weaver writes.

Senate Democrats don’t want a shutdown this fall: Several key caucus members told NOTUS this week that they are open to a short-term stopgap spending measure to get through the election, our Stephen Neukam and Igor Bobic report. Sen. Katie Britt (R-Alabama), an appropriator, said she is “cautiously optimistic” about the status of government funding talks.

From the campaign trail


“I think we might be about to shoot ourselves in the head on this one,” a Michigan Democratic strategist tells NOTUS’ Alex Roarty of the mess centrists have made for themselves in the state’s 7th Congressional District. It’s a top pickup opportunity for Democrats, but the establishment is torn between two candidates, former Navy SEAL Matt Maasdam and onetime Ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink, and risks splitting the vote and handing the nomination to progressive William Lawrence, co-founder of the oft-controversial activism group Sunrise Movement.

Neither centrist has shown any sign of backing down. Progressives are filling up another bowl of popcorn as it all unfolds.

First on NOTUS: More green money for Democrats. The super PAC affiliated with the League of Conservation Voters plans to spend $50 million on the midterms, NOTUS’ Elena Schneider reports. The money will go to help Democratic candidates across the country by targeting voters who feel the affordability pinch, the group told Elena.

Traditional environmentalism has taken a back seat in Democratic messaging this cycle, and the LCV-affiliated PAC is the latest green group to shift their focus to an affordability pitch. Last week, we told you about a Pennsylvania buy from NRDC Action Votes, the political spending group affiliated with the Natural Resources Defense Council, taking a similar approach.

When is a corporate donation not a corporate donation? The Democrats’ pick to challenge Rep. Rob Bresnahan (R-Pennsylvania) in November is running on a pledge against money from corporate PACs. But campaign finance documents show that money is still flowing in for Paige Cognetti, the mayor of Scranton — just indirectly, NOTUS’ Avani Kalra reports. And it’s reviving the long-debated question about PAC money and its role in politics.

Money from noncorporate PAC money is pouring into Congetti’s campaign, but those noncorporate PACs are frequently bankrolled by their corporate partners. Take for example Democratic Sen. entries.title: Centrist Democrats Are Staring Down Disaster in a Michigan Swing District
entries.summary: Two establishment-friendly Democrats are battling it out in Lansing. Unfortunately for them, they’re not alone in the race.
entries.content:
LANSING, Mich. — The Democratic Party establishment is on the verge of another big problem ahead of November’s midterm elections.

In Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, party leaders believe either of two candidates running — former Navy SEAL Matt Maasdam or onetime Ukraine ambassador Bridget Brink — could win the battleground district.

The problem? There’s a third candidate. And Maasdam and Brink have attacked each other relentlessly while drawing from the same pool of supporters — giving a progressive activist a chance to win instead.

Democratic strategists in Michigan and Washington are deeply worried that the party is on the verge of nominating William Lawrence, co-founder of the climate activism group Sunrise Movement. Doing so, they fear, would be an electoral disaster in a swing district — held by Republican Rep. Tom Barrett — that narrowly backed Donald Trump in 2024.

The situation has left some Democrats frustrated at the inability of its centrist and establishment-friendly factions to unify behind one candidate, in the joint goal of blocking a candidate whose unabashedly progressive politics they agree are a poor fit for the district.

“It’s a mess,” said Emily Cherniack, founder and CEO of New Politics, which backs candidates with a service background and has endorsed Maasdam. “People aren’t coalescing to say, ‘This is going to be the candidate because, mission first, we gotta win. That’s not happening.”

Cherniack, in an interview last week, said she expected Lawrence would win, even if he gets far less than 50% of the vote.

On Wednesday, a pro-Maasdam group released a poll showing Lawrence leading the primary field with 38% support, followed by Maasdam in second and Brink in third. Other recent surveys have shown Brink in second place.

Michigan’s 7th District, a mix of suburban and rural communities that includes Lansing, is rated a “toss-up” by The Cook Political Report, and Democrats have targeted it as one of their best chances to flip a GOP-held district in November.

“It’s an insane thing to say about what should be a top-5 pickup opportunity this year, but I think we might be about to shoot ourselves in the head on this one,” said one Democratic strategist in Michigan, who requested anonymity to speak candidly.

It’s the latest instance of the Democratic Party’s sometimes stumbling efforts to block progressive candidates from winning races in key states or districts, one that threatens to complicate its efforts to win congressional majorities in the House and Senate this fall.

In Maine, for instance, progressive newcomer Graham Platner toppled a sitting governor in the state’s Senate primary, before being forced from the race after being accused of sexual assault. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, meanwhile, has faced setbacks in places like California and Arizona, where its preferred candidates lost their primaries.

The DCCC has not publicly expressed a preference in the 7th District race. But other centrist Democratic leaders say the party needs to be able to better navigate races like these, whether led by party committees or the candidates themselves.

“It’s vital that in winnable but tough swing districts, mainstream Democrats take their cues from Amy Klobuchar and Pete Buttigieg and step aside to avoid a more extreme candidate from winning,” said Matt Bennett, co-founder of the center-left Democratic think tank Third Way.

In interviews this week, neither Brink nor Maasdam gave any indication they were planning to step aside, each calling themselves the candidate with the best chance to win a primary and general election.

“It seems a little awkward to have the person who's in the lead of that group drop out of the race to give it to the person who’s not in the lead,” Maasdam told NOTUS in an interview, reflecting his campaign’s belief that he has pulled ahead of Brink and sits within striking distance of Lawrence. “I would say, the person who’s not in the lead should drop out, but that would just be my opinion.”

Brink, whose campaign maintains she leads Maasdam in the polls, said in an interview with NOTUS that it’s a sign of weakness for her opponent’s campaign that outside groups have spent millions of dollars backing his candidacy.

“I am the strongest candidate to win both the primary and the general election,” she said.

The two candidates have continued to attack each other publicly, while outside groups working on their behalf have also launched negative ads against their opponent.

Lawrence has also been the recipient of attack ads from at least one outside group, part of a significant, if belated, effort to siphon support from his campaign. He’s also been the beneficiary of more than $1 million in ads widely believed to be funded by a Republican group, Michigan Sunrise PAC — an effort to meddle in Democratic primaries that the GOP has undertaken in a handful of key districts this year.

Brink and Maasdam have also split the endorsements of local power brokers: Maasdam has the support of Sen. Elissa Slotkin, who held the 7th District seat before running for Senate in 2024 and took the unusual step of appearing in a pro-Maasdam ad. Brink has the support of an array of local Democratic leaders, including former Gov. Jennifer Granholm.

Lawrence has campaigned explicitly on the acrimony between Maasdam and Brink and the deluge of outside spending trying to assist their campaigns. On Tuesday, he said he spent much of the day walking more than 12 miles through Lansing in an effort to talk to voters and business owners about policies that could help make life easier.

“I think the voters are sick of it, and we’ve been running a positive campaign all along, fighting hard for what we believe,” he told NOTUS in an interview. “Not afraid to draw a contrast but keeping it focused on policy rather than baseless, personal attacks, like my two opponents have been throwing at each other.”

Lawrence ended his walk Tuesday at a campaign rally in Lansing, sharing a stage with Abdul El-Sayed, an ideological ally who is himself on the ballot next week as a Senate candidate. Like El-Sayed, Lawrence backs single-payer health care, denounces Israel’s treatment of Palestine, and argues that he represents a fresh start from the failed status-quo politics of yesteryear.

He’s also campaigned aggressively against data centers, an issue he said would help him win over Republican voters in November. Lawrence denied he would be the weakest candidate to face the Republican this fall, saying his opposition to the establishment in both parties will make him an attractive candidate for a wide array of voters.

“The Democrats have let us down so many times, and they also participate in the cover-up of the Epstein files, and they’ve also voted for these endless and pointless wars over the last 25 years,” he said. “And so, I’m not here to play partisan games. I’m not here to play Team Red against Team Blue. I’m here to represent the people of these districts.”

Brink and Maasdam allies say they think their preferred candidate still has at least an outside chance to win, if they’re able to muster a late surge in momentum. But each side is also deeply frustrated with the other.

Maasdam and his allies think he has the late momentum in the race, driven by his military background (Maasdam carried the “nuclear football” for President Barack Obama, a biographical fact supportive groups have cited in ads) and the perception he’d give Democrats a formidable nominee to back in the fall. At a campaign event Wednesday in Williamston, he also made an explicit electoral argument against Lawrence, saying his radical approach to politics won’t sit well with many voters of the district.

“I want work within the bounds the Constitution provides. I think he wants to burn that down,” he said to an audience of about 20 voters. “He’d rather burn it down and start with a new system than to work within the bounds of what we have created in America. And I think that’s the wrong way to go.”

Brink and her allies see the race differently. They believe Maasdam is only competitive because of a relatively late surge of millions of dollars in outside spending, much of which ultimately did more to boost Lawrence’s candidacy than his own.

“What’s happening in our race is that there’s a ton of dark money in this race — it's a kind of super PAC money, and it’s unaccountable,” said Brink, who added that $5 million of the $6 million spent in the primary by outside groups had gone toward helping Maasdam’s campaign. “It’s not transparent.”

entries.title: Texas Immigrant Is First to Face Terrorist Deportation Court
entries.summary: The case against a woman admitted to the United States as a lawful permanent resident in 2018 is the first in the 30-year existence of the Alien Terrorist Removal Court.
entries.content:
The Justice Department awakened a terrorist deportation court this month to remove the mother of an Afghan teenager who was convicted of plotting an ISIS-inspired mass shooting on Election Day in 2024, according to newly released filings.

A public hearing Thursday morning will be the first for the “Alien Terrorist Removal Court,” an untested tribunal also handling its first case in its 30-year existence.

The Justice Department said Nazira Haji Zada, 47, from Fort Worth, Texas, was arrested earlier this week. She is accused of helping plot a planned attack that was to be carried out by her son, Abdullah Haji Zada, who was 17 at the time of his arrest in 2024, and her son-in-law, Nasir Ahmad Tawhedi, 28, a DOJ news release said.

Nazira Zada’s case, detailed in some documents posted on the court’s website late Wednesday, provides the first glimpse into a legal venue where prosecutors can rely on secret evidence — and an accused person does not have the otherwise fundamental right to challenge that it was illegally obtained.

Those documents show that the legal proceeding relies largely on evidence the government has deemed classified, meaning that prosecutors are not willing to make public the materials it’s using to support its accusation.

An unclassified FBI summary of the evidence says Nazira Zada “worked to indoctrinate her children with ISIS ideology” and helped the attackers while keeping it all from her husband. A separate declaration by a high ranking Immigration and Customs Enforcement official says that the woman’s husband was employed from 2009 until 2016 at Bagram Air Base in Afghanistan, a main hub for the United States military during the 20-year war in the country.

That declaration also said Nazira Zada was admitted to the United States as a lawful permanent resident in 2018, as a derivative on her husband’s immigrant visa application.

The case is being overseen by U.S. District Judge Joan Ericksen of Minnesota, who is currently serving as the Alien Terrorist Removal Court’s chief judge. The government’s attempt to move forward on the case earlier this month was slowed down, because Ericksen “had questions about the application and the evidence submitted to support it,” she wrote.

That supplement is also classified, and only the cover page was posted publicly.

The initial status hearing is set to begin at 11 a.m. Thursday at the federal courthouse in Washington, D.C.

DOJ had initially planned to arrest the woman, fly her to the nation’s capital, and present her in court “all within the same day,” according to a court filing. However, a department news release said “Zada was arrested earlier this week.”

That release called Nazira Zada “the matriarch of an alien Afghan family,” and said court documents in the criminal case say that the family, to raise funds for the attack, “started selling off their property, including furniture, computers, a mobile phone, and the family’s two vehicles.”

Government officials say the woman speaks Dari, understands little English and will need an interpreter in court.

“This is a historic step asking this court for the first time to remove an individual from the United States who supported a plot by ISIS-sympathizing family members to commit an act of terrorism in America,” FBI Director Kash Patel said in a prepared statement. “No one should be allowed to come into our country and then betray it. The FBI and our Justice Department partners will not hesitate to use all available resources to protect the American people.”

The ATRC is a deportation proceeding that is civil, not criminal, in nature. It’s yet unclear what evidence the government has to accuse Nazira Zada of assisting her son and son-in-law. Her son, who faced terrorism charges, was sentenced to 15 years in prison after he pleaded guilty to receiving a firearm and ammunition to commit a terrorist attack.

Tawhedi, who is also accused of terrorism, underwent a psychological evaluation and was subsequently committed “for an additional period of evaluation and treatment” as per a judge’s order.

entries.title: Senate Advances Trump’s CDC Picks, With Bill Cassidy Setting Aside Concerns
entries.summary: Cassidy, the Republican chair of the Senate’s health committee, had previously voiced reservations about the picks' abilities to separate themselves from RFK Jr.’s views on vaccines.
entries.content:
Senate Republicans advanced Erica Schwartz’s nomination to lead the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, paving the way for the administration’s pick to be confirmed by the full Senate.

Schwartz, a former chief medical officer of the Coast Guard, served as a deputy U.S. surgeon general during the first Trump administration. Her public health bona fides put her on slightly better footing with the Senate Committee for Health, Education, Labor and Pensions, though the committee’s chair, Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-Louisiana), still pressed Schwartz on whether she would stand up to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

During her confirmation hearing, Schwartz told Cassidy that she would “never betray the science.”

Cassidy, who lost his bid for a third term earlier this year, ultimately said he would support Schwartz after the CDC updated a webpage about vaccines and autism to remove a reference to him.

The web page previously said that it contained the phrase “vaccines do not cause autism” only to appease Cassidy. Last week, that statement was removed, and replaced with: “Scientists have not identified the root causes of autism. HHS continues to support rigorous scientific research and will update this page as reliable new evidence becomes available.”

Cassidy, who has been a critic of Kennedy’s vaccine policies, also supported the nomination of Sean Kaufman to serve as the assistant secretary for preparedness and response. The committee also voted to advance Kaufman’s nomination to the full Senate.

Kaufman’s past comments questioning the safety and efficacy of vaccines drew the senator’s ire during his appearance before HELP.

Cassidy said at the outset of Thursday’s vote that he had received assurances from HHS that Kaufman would not be involved in vaccine policy or be the ultimate decision-maker on issues like mRNA vaccines.

“We can’t have perfection,” Cassidy said. He added that the administration is “committed to continuing to work to remove misinformation” from the CDC web page on vaccines and autism, which remains online. He also said that “several actions have been taken” to address decisions relating to vaccines and autism at HHS, including “key personnel changes and better oversight.”

The CDC has been without a permanent director since last August, when Susan Monarez was ousted for disagreeing with Kennedy on vaccine policy decisions. National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya has served as acting leader of the CDC since then.

entries.title: Trump Keeps Greenlighting Requests to Push Data Centers Off the Grid
entries.summary: The Energy Department is stepping in during severe weather — a sign of the strains of the AI agenda.
entries.content:
It’s happening again. Summer temperatures are soaring in much of the South and Midwest this week, straining the electrical grid. Utility operators reached a conclusion that they, and others, have reached before: To avoid blackouts, they may need to boot data centers off the grid.

The Energy Department has obliged, issuing an order that allows Southwest Power Pool, which operates from Montana to Louisiana, to push data centers to use their own backup generators to reduce demand on the grid.

Since May, the Energy Department has issued this kind of emergency authorization six times for PJM Interconnection, the grid operator that covers much of the mid-Atlantic and part of the Rust Belt, and for Southwest Power Pool. Some of those orders extended previous allowances. Collectively, the utilities operate across 30 states and in areas with the highest concentrations of data centers in the country.

Grid operators say this summer’s heat waves have not forced them to use the authority yet. But as the Trump administration pushes unfettered data center development in pursuit of supersizing the artificial intelligence industry, these emergency orders show the limitations facing that agenda.

The nation’s electrical grids cannot currently sustain such rapid growth.

“It confirms that data centers are significantly increasing demand for electricity,” said Ari Peskoe, the director of the Electricity Law Initiative at Harvard. “During these extremely anomalous days where demand for electricity is at its absolute peak, there can be challenges to supply enough energy to everyone.”

The Energy Department’s authorizations, known as 202(c) orders, have generally been used to allow generators to run as much as they can during emergency conditions such as heat waves or cold snaps, when demand for energy is higher than what the grid can comfortably supply, he said. Generators are then exempt from pollution regulations that would otherwise apply.

But now, DOE is allowing grid operators to direct large power users to turn to their own backup generators during heat waves — with grid operators identifying data centers as some of those large loads.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright began sending out those orders for grid operators during a large storm in January.

PJM — which petitioned the DOE for this kind of authorization over the winter, in May and twice in July — said it has not actually implemented the order, and no data centers or other large power users have been required to move to backup generation.

In early July, when PJM’s system set a record for electric demand, the grid operator issued a warning to data centers and other large users to be prepared to switch to backup generators within 15 minutes, but they didn’t ultimately need to take that step.

SPP, the other utility that has received emergency permission to put data centers on backup generation this summer, also said it has not used that authority yet. If weather conditions improve this week as expected, SPP says it anticipates returning to normal operating conditions.

The orders are “probably a win-win,” Peskoe said. It may cost data centers to turn on their backup generators, but it’s a way to avoid outages and any associated public relations nightmares.

There are downsides, however. Backup generators emit more emissions than power from the grid does. Turning to them could result in more pollutants in the communities where data centers are located.

The emissions from emergency situations are not counted toward a facility’s emissions limits.

Asking data centers to turn on their generators during heat waves isn’t a long-term solution, said Junbo Zhao, an associate professor of engineering at Dartmouth who studies power systems.

More energy generation and reliance on new grid technologies that help manage congestion could help avoid the kinds of problems grid operators have faced this summer. And, Zhao said, there needs to be more coordination among data centers and grid operators.

“Data centers are operating their data centers, and operators are trying to assess whether data centers are going to affect reliability,” he said. “They don’t have dedicated coordination with each other to improve the efficiency and reliability of the grid.”

Data centers must go through an interconnection process, which is meant to ensure they won’t threaten the grid’s reliability. But the grid isn’t prepared for the number of new, massive energy users that have come online in the past couple of years.

Last week in Virginia, PJM got a taste of the grid-destabilizing power of data centers when a group of facilities in Northern Virginia abruptly unplugged from the grid and transferred to backup power, putting about 3% of electric demand offline and changing the grid’s frequency.

Reuters reported that voltage disturbances extended all the way to Chicago.

To deal with the issue of power-hungry data centers during heat waves and other events that are stressful for the grid, PJM is proposing to create a registry of large energy users that would track where they are and whether they brought their own energy supply to the grid.

During grid emergencies, PJM could force large users to go off the grid and onto backup generators, or to reduce their power use, if they haven’t brought their own generators to the system.

That proposal dovetails with the Trump administration’s push for data centers to bring, buy or build their own power — a strategy to keep the cost of running that infrastructure from being charged to all ratepayers.

entries.title: European Soccer Plans to Boycott FIFA Competitions Over Private Investments
entries.summary: “The World Cup is not for sale,” the European association said after news that Jared Kushner’s brother may be eyeing a stake in the tournament.
entries.content:
The governing body of European soccer voted to boycott international competitions hosted by FIFA after its president, Gianni Infantino, announced plans to allow private investors to buy stakes in the World Cup.

FIFA said it would open up the tournament to private investment on Wednesday, after Infantino reportedly ran the plans by officials in President Donald Trump’s administration. Joshua Kushner — the brother of Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner — has been considered a potential key investor in the proposal, and other figures within Trump’s orbit have been involved, sources told The Times of London, which first reported on the plans.

“The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product,” the Union of European Football Associations wrote in a statement. “No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale.”

The coalition said its 55 nations “stand as one” and voted “unanimously and unequivocally to reject FIFA’s proposal.”

“The FIFA World Cup belongs to football and always will,” The Football Association, the governing body of association football in England wrote on X, backing UEFA’s decision.

FIFA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

UEFA said none of its teams will participate in any future matches unless they have assurances that Infantino will block FIFA competitions from future private ownership. The 2030 World Cup is scheduled to take place across stadiums in Spain, Portugal and Morocco.

FIFA hopes to raise up to $4.2 billion in private-sector capital for a new organization that would oversee key business aspects of major soccer tournaments like the World Cup.

Infantino’s proposal would open up a new subsidiary, FIFA Forward Enterprise, in which select third-party companies could invest in competitions. FIFA, which overwhelmingly controls the global soccer network, has approached Joshua Kushner’s Thrive Capital and is partnering with J.P. Morgan.

Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee blasted reports of discussions between FIFA and Trump’s administration on Tuesday, when the news broke about Infantino’s plans to sell shares.

“Infantino is trying to bribe every member country in FIFA with a $40 million payoff to sign off on his scheme to turn the World Cup into a get-rich-quick extraction industry for oligarchs and billionaires,” the Judiciary Democrats’ account said on X. “It’s time for everyone who loves soccer to oppose this sinister.”

Trump and Infantino have enjoyed a close relationship, with the FIFA president making frequent visits to the White House and Mar-a-Lago. Trump presented the World Cup Trophy on July 19 in New Jersey, a few months after Infantino awarded him the newly created “FIFA Peace Prize” in December.

Infantino set a Sept. 19 deadline for the 211 federations to approve the plans. The controversial FIFA initiative would give each of them access to $40 million in funding, ESPN reported.

Other multinational soccer governing bodies are still reviewing Infantino’s plans. The Confederation of African Football is set to hold a meeting of its executive committee next week to evaluate FIFA’s proposal.
