entries.title: Palestinian Authorities Petition SCOTUS to Stave Off Massive Legal Judgment
entries.summary: They argue the massive $650 million penalty will destabilize critical government services in the West Bank.
entries.content:
Palestinian authorities filed an application with the Supreme Court on Thursday in a last-ditch attempt to block a more than $650 million judgment against the groups, which they say would result in the loss of critical services, cause untold human suffering and destabilize the war-torn region even further.

On March 30, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit reinstated a $655.5 million judgment against the Palestine Liberation Organization and Palestinian Authority in an Anti-Terrorism Act case brought by U.S. victims and survivors of terrorist attacks in Israel.

The Palestine Liberation Organization is the internationally recognized representative body for the Palestinian people, and the Palestinian Authority was created by the PLO in the 1990s to manage civil and security affairs in parts of the West Bank. The United States does not officially recognize either as a terror organization today. However, in 1987 Congress passed the Anti-Terrorism Act, labeling the PLO as a “terrorist organization and a threat to the interests of the US.”

The PLO does have a history of armed conflict against Israel, and while the Palestinian Authority was created to be a governing body committed to a diplomatic framework, elements within it have engaged in localized violence.

The Oct. 7, 2023, attacks, led by Hamas, triggered a war in Gaza that has severely destabilized the West Bank, resulting in a surge of military raids, Israeli settler violence, economic distress and heightened political friction for the Palestinian Authority.

Now, the PLO and the Palestinian Authority are arguing the multimillion-dollar judgment against them will only make the situation in the area worse, saying that civic life is hanging “by a thread” in the West Bank.

“Immediate enforcement of the $655.5 million judgment may cut that thread, depriving millions of people of government services they depend on, and which provide security and stability for Israel, Palestine, and the region alike,.” the briefing reads. “The security, sanitation, and school services provided by Petitioners in the West Bank are hanging by a thread.”

The judgment against both groups was initially rendered after a jury verdict in 2015, but it was subsequently vacated in 2016 on the ground that U.S. courts lacked personal jurisdiction over the defendants. In response, Congress enacted new legislation, dubbed the “Promoting Security and Justice for Victims of Terrorism Act,” designed to enable jurisdiction in similar cases.

Following the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in Fuld v. Palestine Liberation Organization, which confirmed that the congressional act is compatible with the Fifth Amendment, the case returned to the Second Circuit, which agreed to recall its earlier mandate, effectively undoing its 2016 ruling.

The application submitted by the PLO and the Palestinian Authority to halt the lower court’s order is up to the discretion of the Supreme Court itself, which has a history of accepting fewer than 1% of appeals in similar cases, according to Justice Department data.

entries.title: RFK Jr. Launches a MAHA Cooking Show
entries.summary: He’s the second Cabinet member to star in a web show during Trump’s second term.
entries.content:
Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. launched an online cooking show on Thursday that aims to teach to teach Americans that making healthy meals can be “delicious and affordable,” according to the show’s splashy new web page.

The slickly produced program is part of the Health Department’s “Eat Real Food” initiative, which dramatically reshaped the country’s dietary guidelines earlier this year in alignment with Kennedy’s “Make America Healthy Again” agenda.

The new guidelines effectively flipped the long-standing food pyramid to prioritize meat, dairy and vegetables over refined foods and grains. The guidelines also endorsed consumption of saturated fats that contradict established nutrition advice to limit them.

The American Medical Association praised the guidelines, which shifted standards for school lunches and food stamps, for its straightforward advice on eating whole foods.

Kennedy, an ardent critic of ultra-processed foods, has continually targeted what he claims are the catalysts of childhood chronic disease: sugary products, environmental toxins, Wi-Fi radiation and medications, including vaccines and antidepressants.

Kennedy’s first stop on his cooking show brought him to Huntington Beach, California, where Andrew Gruel, a city council member, chef and conservative political commentator, joined the show as its first special guest. Thursday’s premiere episode was not entirely devoid of politics.

Between a lesson on how to cook crispy salmon cakes, Kennedy inserted talking points about why Americans don’t eat enough seafood.

“I think it’s cultural because we have a lot of seafood in this country, and we’re used to eating meat, and think of that as our protein. Today we have the lowest level of cattle herds in history, in at least 100 years,” he said. “The cost of meat has gone up, we’re doing everything that we can in the administration to bring that down and increase the size of the herd.”

As he mixed avocado mayonnaise into a mixing bowl, Kennedy took a moment to slam the “war” on saturated fats and the previous dietary guidelines that had been workshopped by the Biden administration.

“They were 453-pages long, and they were entirely written by food industry lobbyists,” Kennedy said. “They reflected the same kind of mercantile impulses that had put Fruit Loops at the top of the food pyramid.”

Kennedy is the second Trump Cabinet member to launch his own show. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced in March that he was launching an online series dubbed “The Great American Road Trip,” in which he and his family traveled cross-country to various American landmarks.

Democrats panned Duffy’s show as a prepaid vacation that distracted Duffy from important work in Washington. The series was also scrutinized for ethical concerns over its sponsors, which included several companies regulated by the Transportation Department, including Toyota and Boeing.

Despite an extensive marketing campaign announcing the program’s release, the show has not premiered yet and Duffy said in May he would not record any more episodes.

HHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment about who is footing the bill for the show’s production and how much it has cost to make.
entries.author: Angie Orellana Hernandez

entries.title: Trump: I'm Fine Withdrawing Blanche Until Tillis and Cornyn Leave Office
entries.summary: Trump said the pair of senators were withholding their votes as an act of retaliation after the president refused to endorse them.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump said he had “no objection” to temporarily withdrawing Todd Blanche’s nomination for attorney general until Republican Sens. John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina leave office.

The pair, who lost bitterly contested primaries after Trump opted not to back them, have refused to vote for Blanche over concerns that he and the Justice Department have not done enough to kill a proposed $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund for Trump’s political allies and a deal shielding the president and his businesses from future tax audits.

Trump claimed on Truth Social Thursday that Cornyn and Tillis were withholding their key votes as retaliation for their losses in primary elections earlier this year.

“John Cornyn, of Texas, and Thom Tillis, of North Carolina, both of whom I refused to Endorse, and whose political careers have been ended by my action, are refusing to vote for this Great Nominee, who will remain, in any event, as Acting,” Trump wrote. “I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd’s name, if they do not do the right thing, and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office.”

Cornyn suggested on social media after Trump’s post that there were additional lawmakers who also had similar concerns about Trump’s settlement with the IRS that was signed by Blanche. Cornyn’s post did not indicate whether any other concerned parties were also considering voting no on his confirmation.

Cornyn told reporters on Thursday that Trump attributing the stalled vote to an act of revenge was a “convenient excuse, but it’s certainly not true.”

The Texas Republican called off a meeting with Blanche on Wednesday, alleging that the Justice Department was not “responsive” to his requests. Cornyn said he sent the Justice Department line-by-line edits to its proposal on the audit exemption deal and the $1.776 billion “anti-weaponization” fund that would compensate individuals whom the federal government investigated under the Biden administration.

The Senate Judiciary Committee delayed advancing a vote for Blanche’s confirmation on Wednesday evening, stating that Cornyn and Tillis wanted written assurance from the Justice Department.

Tillis said Thursday he still saw a path forward in the negotiations, but that he did not “understand all of this drama.”

“Everybody's saying that it's just a few details to sort out the audit. Well, why on Earth is the president now weighing in and saying no, unless somebody's told him that maybe you want to keep these vehicles in place because you could use them someday?” Tillis told reporters. “That is a horrible look. You can't explain it. … If I were running, there's no way I could excuse this or explain it.”

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R–South Dakota) said Thursday that the best strategy to confirm Blanche required resolving Cornyn’s and Tillis’ questions.

“I'll defer to whatever the White House and president decide they want to do,” he said.

Senator Dick Durbin (D–Illinois), the ranking member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, said Trump’s threat to pull Blanche’s nomination rather than change the settlement indicated the president was “trying up the pressure” against the duo so that they change their position.

Durbin said he had “no doubt” that concerns about the settlement were more widespread in the Republican Party — but that others were “afraid to say the first word about it.”

“These two senators, like me, are lame ducks, and they have more courage to deal with these issues than their colleagues,” Durbin said.

entries.title: Trump-Themed Passport Rollout Goes National
entries.summary: An additional 250,000 “Patriot Passports” will soon be available at more than two dozen passport agencies across the country.
entries.content:
The State Department plans to make a new batch of U.S. passports with President Donald Trump’s image available nationwide, citing an “overwhelming demand” for special editions of the travel document.

“Americans all across the country will now have the opportunity to apply for one of these additional special passports, known as the ‘Patriot Passport,’” the State Department wrote in a statement.

The passports were originally only available for in-person applicants at the Washington Passport Agency in D.C. The State Department is set to make an additional 250,000 accessible from 27 passport agencies across the country beginning Aug. 8. Appointments are required to apply.

“An American passport is more than just a travel document; it's a physical piece of our national identity – a reminder that wherever you are in the world, you are an American,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio wrote on X about the expanded offering of the travel documents.

No living president has ever been featured on a passport prior to Trump’s rollout this year in commemoration of the nation’s 250th anniversary.

“Patriot Passports” are some of the latest government-produced items to feature Trump’s image. The U.S. Mint has started production for $1 coins emblazoned with his portrait that are expected to be released into circulation this fall. The president’s signature will also appear on paper bills, with the currency set to roll out later this year. In Congress, Republicans introduced a bill in February to include Trump’s portrait on $250 bills to celebrate the nation’s founding.

The passports have commemorative artwork honoring America’s 250th anniversary, including a portrait of Trump within the text of the Declaration of Independence on the inside cover and a picture of John Trumbull’s famous “Declaration of Independence” painting on the back cover.

The travel documents also have a gold Freedom 250 flag — representing the Trump-backed group that organized events in Washington like July’s Great American State Fair and and an upcoming Grand Prix race. Freedom 250 took over celebrations of the nation's founding, leaving the bipartisan, congressionally funded group America 250 largely out of this summer’s major events.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Defense Hawks Challenge the White House Push for a Narrow Reconciliation Bill
entries.summary: The Senate Armed Services chair says roughly $300 billion is needed for “this generational investment.”
entries.content:
Senate defense hawks are pushing back on the White House plan for a narrowly tailored reconciliation bill, warning that Republicans may have only one opportunity to finance President Donald Trump’s military buildup and demanding far more than the House’s $60 billion defense proposal.

The fight is complicating Senate Majority Leader John Thune’s effort to cobble together 50 Republican votes before the Senate adjourns next week until mid-September. Republicans broadly agree the Pentagon needs significantly more money, but they are divided over whether the next reconciliation bill should cover only immediate needs or finance a sweeping military buildup.

Senate Armed Services Committee Chair Roger Wicker (R-Mississippi) said the package should include roughly $300 billion for defense — roughly five times the House instruction — while other hawks urged Republican leaders to increase the number substantially.

“We need something close to $300 billion for this generational investment, to defend ourselves in the world against the axis of aggression,” Wicker said.

The push runs counter to fiscally conservative Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought’s pitch for a narrow bill, with the remainder of Trump’s $1.5 trillion military budget request deferred to a later reconciliation package.

“It should be tight,” Vought told reporters after meeting with Senate Republicans this week. “It should be for the defense needs that we need now, for the [agriculture] needs that we need now, and to get this as straight a shot to the president's desk as possible.”House Speaker Mike Johnson, along these lines, sent the Senate the House’s $95 billion reconciliation bill by striking a delicate balance between defense hawks in his conference and fiscal conservatives wary of adding billions to the deficit. Offsetting the new spending could require politically painful spending cuts just ahead of November’s elections.

Thune has signaled that the House’s defense number is likely to be too low for his members. He told reporters he would “prefer doubling” it as Republican leaders search for enough votes to advance the measure.

But Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson (R-Wisconsin), a fiscal hawk whose committee would spearhead the reconciliation bill, poured cold water on the defense increase. He said Thune had not mentioned it to him.

“White House is trying to skinny it down for passage, so we’ll see,” Johnson said. “I know there's a desire on the part of many to increase those numbers. Again, we'll have to figure out what the conference wants to do here.”

The unresolved questions come amid growing alarm over the Iran war’s toll on U.S. munitions stockpiles, which are being further depleted because of Trump’s fresh escalation in the conflict.

The Pentagon on Wednesday signed a $56 billion contract with Lockheed Martin for Patriot interceptors, but the money for that and other budget priorities, such as Golden Dome missile defenses, requires congressional approval.

“You look at munitions — you look at Golden Dome — that are in reconciliation; time is running out,” said Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Nebraska), a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee.
entries.author: Joe Gould, Avani Kalra

entries.title: ABC Fires Back at FCC Over ‘Attempted Censorship’
entries.summary: The network argued the Trump administration is retaliating against it for exercising its First Amendment rights.
entries.content:
ABC News accused the Trump administration of attempting to censor the network in a new regulatory filing responding to the Federal Communications Commission's decision to review the broadcast licenses of its owned-and-operated television stations years before they are set to expire.

The television network, which has been targeted by the FCC because of its programming and on-air comments, argues the administration “is retaliating against ABC for the exercise of its First Amendment rights.”

“The retaliation against ABC is a signal to every media company in the country: accommodate the Administration’s view of what news coverage should look like or pay the price,” the 119-page filing said.

The administration first singled out the network for allegedly violating equal employment opportunity law in March 2025. Later that year, the administration took issue with comments made by late night host Jimmy Kimmel, after which Trump called for Kimmel’s firing.

“We can do this the easy way or the hard way,” FCC chairman Brendan Carr told ABC in September 2025. “These companies can find ways to take action on Kimmel, or there is going to be additional work for the FCC ahead.”

The station’s renewal cycle was not set to begin until 2028, according to the FCC.

Some of the stations the FCC wants to review are based in cities including New York City, Los Angeles, and Chicago. Individual viewers have submitted more than 150,000 comments concerning the “untimely” license renewal request — 96% of which are supportive of ABC, the network says.

Carr’s actions have sparked concern even among some of its staunchest allies. Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) described Carr’s comments to the network as “dangerous as hell.”

Former FCC chairs who served under Democratic and Republican administrations also bashed his leadership, calling his decision to review licensing agreements “an assault on free speech.”

“The Chairman has prejudged the outcome of this proceeding and that the Commission may assert the power to terminate the stations’ licenses early,” the former chairs wrote in a letter to the FCC on Tuesday. “All this betrays that this proceeding is pretext for the Chairman’s continued campaign of suppressing disfavored speech.”

In December 2024, ABC settled a $15 million lawsuit Trump filed against the network over a “This Week” segment in which the host asserted that the president had been found liable for raping writer E. Jean Carroll. A jury found Trump liable for sexual abuse in May 2023.
entries.author: Raymond Fernández

entries.title: Judge Appears Skeptical of Trump Administration’s Arguments About Anthropic Posing Security Threat
entries.summary: Judge Rita F. Lin said at Thursday’s hearing that the record “in some ways, has gotten worse for the government.”
entries.content:
A federal judge said Thursday that the Trump administration’s case against Anthropic had “gotten worse,” sharply questioning whether officials labeled the AI company a national security threat because it had publicly criticized the government.

“I don’t see additional evidence from the government really justifying what it did,” U.S. District Judge Rita F. Lin said at the start of a hearing in the lawsuit the company brought against the administration. “If anything, it seems like the record, in some ways, has gotten worse for the government.”

Anthropic sued after the Pentagon designated it a national security supply chain risk and the administration moved to cut it off from federal work. The company says officials retaliated after it resisted efforts to remove restrictions on using its Claude models for domestic surveillance of Americans and lethal autonomous warfare.

The lawsuit seeks to overturn the designation and prevent the administration from excluding the company from federal contracting. Lin made the comments during a 2.5-hour hearing Thursday in California, where she was considering motions from each side to decide the lawsuit in their favor at this early stage in the case.

Lin said she saw no evidence Anthropic could alter its AI models after delivery, flip a kill switch or seed them beforehand with a hidden control mechanism. She also said she saw no specific reason to suspect the company would do any of those things.

Instead, Lin said, the record appeared to show that Anthropic’s public criticism of the Defense Department caused the administration to lose trust in the company.

“I find that position, if that’s really what the government’s position is, to be really troubling,” Lin said. “It seems at odds to me with the First Amendment, with Section 3252,” the statute the administration relied on to designate the company a national security supply chain risk. 

She later described the government’s apparent position as “quite extreme.”

Lin also questioned whether President Donald Trump had evidence that Anthropic posed a security threat when he first publicly targeted the company on Feb. 27.

“For me, looking at the record doesn’t look like as of February 27th, there’s any information in the record about what Anthropic could or couldn’t do, or whether it posed a threat,” Lin said.

The risk analysis cited by the government was dated March 2, after Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth issued their directives against Anthropic. The company has argued that a memo prepared later could not justify actions officials had already taken.

Lin questioned whether the government had shown any specific reason to believe Anthropic would place hidden restrictions in future models.

“What are the specific articulable facts that suggest Anthropic might sabotage its software in this way?” she asked.

Justice Department lawyer James Harlow pointed to several things, including Anthropic’s refusal to permit all lawful uses, an executive’s questions about Claude’s use during an overseas military operation and concerns about the company’s handling of sensitive information.

Anthropic’s attorneys said none of those showed an intent to interfere with military operations. The company also noted that it had offered contract language promising not to do so.

Anthropic lawyer Michael Mongan argued that the government had shifted from its previously stated concerns about interference with deployed models to the possibility of hidden restrictions inserted before delivery.

That “shifting of rationales” was “powerful evidence of pretext” and weakened the government’s defense against Anthropic’s First Amendment and Administrative Procedure Act claims, he said.

Lin previously issued a preliminary injunction blocking parts of the administration’s actions.

The Pentagon continues to wind down its use of Anthropic products and expects to finish by Sept. 30, Harlow told the court. Several pilot programs at other agencies are scheduled to expire Aug. 30.

Mongan said most agencies had continued working with Anthropic, two had paused negotiations for new contracts, and others were negotiating new deals. He said the company was not aware of any agency canceling a contract after the injunction.

The Justice Department declined to say in open court whether any agencies had increased their use of Claude for national security work since the injunction.

Lin said that conduct could shed light on the government’s original intent and that she may order the parties to provide more information.

Anthropic and the Justice Department have each asked Lin to resolve the case through summary judgment, arguing that there are no material factual disputes that require a trial.

Lin did not rule at Thursday’s hearing. She took the competing motions under submission and said she would issue a written order.
entries.author: Hamed Ahmadi

entries.title: The Commanders’ Defense Has Made a Strong First Impression at Camp
entries.summary: The offense? Not so much.
entries.content:
Commanders defensive coordinator Daronte Jones had a simple message for his unit ahead of Thursday's training camp practice: “They don’t get in the fucking end zone.”

Two days into camp, it’s clear Jones’ players have taken heed. The defense has mostly smothered the offense so far, both starters and reserves. Facing a relentless pass rush and suffocating coverage, Washington’s offense has struggled to move the ball, let alone reach the end zone.

This defensive unit was slow and aged just a year ago, so the front office went out and signed eight players in free agency, hoping the group could become faster and more versatile. Based on first impressions in Ashburn, that effort appears to be paying off already.

“When you look at this roster … the firepower we got, guys coming off the edge, guys all the way on the front seven, guys we got flying around in the back end — the sky's the limit,” veteran safety Will Harris said.

It’s hard to decide who or what has stood out most for the defense since training camp kicked off Wednesday. The line and edge rushers, particularly free agent signee Odafe Oweh, have practically moved into the offensive backfield and declared squatter’s rights. Oweh stuffed multiple plays on Day 1 and swatted down a pass from quarterback Jayden Daniels, while fellow linebackers Jordan Magee and K’Lavon Chaisson (another new face) have made their way into the backfield on multiple run plays. Safety Nick Cross (also new) blitzed Daniels at one point to blow up a pass play.

“When we put it all together, it’s going to be a masterpiece,” linebacker Frankie Luvu said. “I'm excited for the guys up front — we got some dogs. We holding them back right now because we ain't got the pads on, but when it’s time to let them loose we’ll have a lot of splash plays in the backfield.”

In coverage, new cornerbacks Ahkello Witherspoon and Amik Robertson have looked solid. Rookie linebacker Sonny Styles — picked seventh overall in large part because of his elite athleticism — has stayed hip-to-hip, stride-for-stride with his assignments like he’s their ballroom dance partner.

The defense nabbed two interceptions Thursday, one by undrafted free agent Malik Spencer early in the session and a would-be pick-6 by newly signed corner Rasul Douglas on the final play of the day.

During two-minute drills, the defense forced three field goals after stuffing the offense on third down.

“We bring in those guys that come in and get after the quarterback,” Daniels said Wednesday about the new defensive linemen. “It's good work on both sides that at the end of the day, that's all camp really is. Building our identity, making sure guys get good work, make each other better.”

On the other side of the ball, the offense is going through the growing pains expected of a unit run by a first-time playcaller implementing a new system.

The group has looked out of sorts at times. The receivers have been a source of much debate this offseason and that uncertainty hasn’t been quelled in these early days. They have consistently struggled to gain separation.

The defense “had a really good day. I'm not afraid to say that,” veteran receiver Terry McLaurin said Thursday. “But, that's camp. There's gonna be back and forth.”

You can see the vision that coordinator David Blough has for his unit: lots of pre-snap motion and shifts; quarterbacks alternating from shotgun to under center; plenty of play action to hold the defense. It just hasn’t led to immediate success.

Ahead of Wednesday’s practice, coach Dan Quinn said he expected early mistakes from the offense, but hoped to see less and less as camp progresses.

“I just wanna see the execution, guys functioning at a high level together,” Quinn said.

On Wednesday, there were highlight throws to receivers Antonio Williams, Jaden Bradley and Treylon Burks, who hauled in multiple difficult touchdown catches. (Burks missed Thursday’s practice due to foot soreness.)

Tight end Chig Okonkwo found success on back-to-back out routes Thursday while receiver Luke McCaffrey shook free from cornerback Mike Sainristil for an impressive toe-tapping touchdown grab in the back of the end zone.

When Daniels or his backups have had time, they’ve made quick and accurate throws. It’s just that those moments have come few and far between.

But, as most players have emphasized, it’s only been two practices and the sky has not fallen.

“It's just Day 2,” McLaurin said Thursday. “It's good to have guys out there flying around. The juice is what I'm super excited about, the competitiveness. We shake [hands] with guys after practice. I didn't really wanna shake up with anybody because we got beat. That's how I am. But at the end of the day, we're still brothers. We're going back and forth, but we still have ‘Commanders’ across our chest, so that's the main thing.”

entries.title: Rep. Ryan Mackenzie Returns Donation From Pardoned Republican Megadonor
entries.summary: The Republican congressman from Pennsylvania received a contribution from Adam Kidan three days before Trump pardoned him.
entries.content:
Rep. Ryan Mackenzie (R-Pennsylvania) returned a donation to a man convicted of fraud in connection with the Jack Abramoff lobbying scandal following reporting that President Donald Trump pardoned him just three days after the contribution.

NOTUS reported Wednesday that Adam Kidan donated $2,600 to Mackenzie’s leadership PAC on June 30, according to Federal Election Commission records. Trump had traveled to Mackenzie’s district on June 23 to campaign alongside the congressman. Trump pardoned Kidan on July 3.

Mackenzie’s returned donation was first reported by The Morning Call.

A spokesperson for Mackenzie did not immediately respond to requests for comment from NOTUS about returning the contribution but told The Morning Call that the congressman returned the donation “to avoid even an appearance of impropriety.”

Arnaud Armstrong, a spokesperson for Mackenzie, previously told NOTUS that Mackenzie “has never advocated for a pardon from the President on anyone’s behalf.”

Kidan donated to Mackenzie’s leadership PAC, a fundraising vehicle often used to contribute money to other like-minded candidates and political committees, and it is the most recent donation Kidan has made, according to FEC records.
AdamKidan (1860x2816, AR: 0.66)Mackenzie, who represents Pennsylvania’s 7th Congressional District, is facing off against Democrat Bob Brooks in one of the most contested House races in the country, which the Cook Political Report ranks a “toss up.”

Kidan served more than two years in prison beginning in 2006 after pleading guilty to conspiracy and wire fraud. He is a notable campaign donor in Pennsylvania and throughout the nation, contributing to Republicans locked in other contested Pennsylvania races, such as Reps. Rob Bresnahan, Brian Fitzpatrick and Scott Perry.

He has donated millions of dollars to Republican causes over the years and gave more than $200,000 to Trump-affiliated committees ahead of the 2024 election cycle, federal records show.

Kidan and Abramoff were ordered to pay $217 million in restitution as part of their sentencing. It remains unclear whether Kidan paid the full amount, and Trump’s pardon is likely to erase any remaining obligations.

entries.title: Mandela Barnes Drops Out of Chaotic Wisconsin Governor's Race
entries.summary: The former lieutenant governor exited as the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel said it was looking into allegations of sexual impropriety.
entries.content:
Former Lt. Gov Mandela Barnes dropped out of the crowded and chaotic Democratic gubernatorial primary in Wisconsin on Thursday.

Shortly after he dropped out, the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reported that it was looking into allegations that Barnes had used his position to have “sexual encounters with young adult women.” The outlet initially provided few other details, adding only that it was continuing to report on the story.

The Journal Sentinel soon updated its story to add that the state Democratic Party hired a law firm last year to look into “similar claims,” but the information it received was “anonymous and unspecific” and was not actionable. The outlet also reported that the Democrat has not been accused of committing crimes.

“There are no allegations of misconduct or wrongdoing against Mandela," a campaign spokesperson told NOTUS.

Barnes’ statement announcing that he was suspending his campaign did not address the Journal Sentinel’s reporting.

“Last night I had a very difficult conversation with my staff,” he said in a video posted on X. “We’re incredibly proud of all the things that we’ve accomplished and all the resources that we have raised to spread our message, but it’s become very clear who our nominee is going to be.”

Leading the pack in the race is Francesca Hong, a state representative and democratic socialist. She has gained momentum in the final weeks of the primary campaign, with one poll by Marquette University Law School showing her more than 20 percentage points ahead of Barnes.

He did not explicitly endorse Hong in his announcement, but said he would work to help defeat Rep. Tom Tiffany, who is leading the Republican field.

That leaves four Democratic candidates ahead of the Aug. 11 primary, a race that is being closely followed given that it’s playing out in a battleground state.

Barnes’ exit is yet another shakeup in a primary in which Lt. Gov Sara Rodriguez dropped out after she reported “serious mismanagement and inaccuracies” in her financial campaign filings. That prompted Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, who had already dropped out of the governor’s race because his campaign was not gaining traction, to reenter with Gov. Tony Evers’ endorsement.

Hong’s rise as the primary’s front-runner is being closely watched, as it’s a test of democratic socialists’ political strength outside of solidly blue districts and states.

Early voting is already underway in Wisconsin, which has created another twist in the race. On Wednesday, the Dane County circuit judge ruled that voters who had cast absentee ballots for Rodriguez would not be able to request new ones — a decision likely to apply to voters who cast ballots for Barnes too.

Democrats in the state were already concerned about Barnes’ electability. From the outset, his gubernatorial bid was haunted by his failed Senate run in 2022, when he lost to Sen. Ron Johnson by just 1 percentage point in a year that Evers won reelection by more than 3 percentage points.

Until his announcement, Barnes’ social media accounts hadn’t otherwise posted since Wednesday. Door-knocking events scheduled for Saturday still appeared on his campaign website, and his social media accounts encouraged supporters to vote early on Wednesday.

Editor’s note: This story has been updated with additional reporting.

entries.title: Senate Considering a Delay in SNAP Cost Shift to States
entries.summary: “I think what we’re looking at is possibly a short-term extension,” Sen. John Boozman said.
entries.content:
The chair of the Senate Agriculture Committee said Thursday he is considering some respite for states that must start sharing costs under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.

Sen. John Boozman (R-Arkansas) told NOTUS the issue is part of negotiations with Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minnesota), the panel’s ranking member, on a way forward on the Senate’s version of a farm bill.

Democrats have asked for a two-year delay in the cost shift to states with SNAP payment error rates above 6%, an increase scheduled to start next year. Republicans have preferred to leave the changes made to SNAP in a 2025 reconciliation law.

“I think what we’re looking at is possibly a short-term extension,” Boozman told NOTUS.

“We’ve been talking to Sen. Klobuchar, talking to the administration, seeing if the time we’ve given is adequate. Nothing has been finalized,” he said.

Boozman didn’t specify how long a delay could be, only referring to it as “short-term.”

Boozman has said the committee will mark up the farm bill late next week. Boozman’s office said the final version of the Senate farm bill is still being worked through but will be released soon.

Klobuchar previously said she was having “productive negotiations” on the farm bill. Her office said Thursday there was nothing to add, but that “there is a lot of work left to do.”

Only 9 states and the Virgin Islands had error rates below the 6% threshold. The changes in the reconciliation law require states to pay for a portion of the implementation of SNAP if their error rate exceeds that level.

“What we want to do is make sure that we have rules that states can actually get. I think the states understand, and they are working really hard to get their error rates down,” Boozman said.

Sen. Jim Justice (R-West Virginia), a member of the committee, welcomed the potential delay. West Virginia’s error rate in 2025 was just above 6%.

“There are states that are going to be so impacted, it’s unbelievable. And West Virginia is going to get hit to the tune of tens of millions,” Justice told NOTUS. “I think what we need is a graduated runway. But working together and having some form of extension, with all the other stuff that we want on our side, I think that’s the way to go.”

West Virginia is just one of many Republican states facing high payments for their error rates. Boozman’s home state of Arkansas sits at above 8%, and several mayors in the state have called on Boozman to provide an extension and protect SNAP more broadly.

Other Republicans on the committee weren’t immediately sold by the idea. Sen. John Hoeven (R-North Dakota) told NOTUS that the idea would land in the “we’ll see column.”
